item.title: 语言的腐败：被操纵的词语如何掩盖真相、侵蚀道德并钝化心智
item.description:
The Corruption of Language: How Manipulated Words Conceal Truth, Erode Morality, and Dull the Mind

A research essay on the concept of “language corruption” (语言腐败)

Abstract

Language corruption denotes the deliberate manipulation, distortion, or redefinition of words in order to conceal truth, whitewash wrongdoing, evade responsibility, and control public opinion. This essay synthesizes a coherent intellectual lineage—running from George Orwell’s Politics and the English Language (1946) and the Newspeak apparatus of Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), through William Lutz’s taxonomy of “doublespeak” and George Lakoff’s theory of framing, to the Chinese economist Zhang Weiying’s (张维迎) explicit 2012 formulation of 语言腐败—and grounds it in contemporary moral psychology. Across these thinkers a single convergent thesis emerges: euphemistic, inflated, or redefined language is engineered to “defend the indefensible,” and degraded language does not merely reflect degraded thought but actively produces it. Albert Bandura’s theory of moral disengagement names euphemistic labeling as a core mechanism by which harmful conduct is cognitively restructured into something benign, and recent large-sample experiments demonstrate that this effect is causal and only partly correctable by conscious effort. The essay closes by examining the harms—eroded communication, dulled reasoning, moral decay, and social unpredictability—and the principal institutional remedy, the plain-language movement, exemplified by the U.S. Plain Writing Act of 2010.
